paras: The lynching of Henry Thomas was the hanging of a Black man near Parish, Manatee County, Florida, on the night of Sunday, March 8, 1903, after citizen posses captured him on an accusation of attempting to criminally assault the ten-year-old daughter of Porter Keene. An Associated Press dispatch from Tampa said he was hanged to a tree after the girl identified him and after he "admitted his guilt," a claim that rests on that account alone. White newspapers across the country carried the dispatch within days, and two Black weeklies later included Thomas in a published record of the year's lynchings.

According to the wire account, on the preceding Friday Keene's ten-year-old daughter was sent to a neighbor's farm half a mile away to buy vegetables. There, the dispatch said, a Black man followed her and attempted to assault her within sight of the farmhouse, and she escaped and ran toward home with him in pursuit. Mrs. Keene, who had gone out to look for her daughter, was reported to have been met by the man with a drawn pistol and a threat to shoot if she came closer. Only the Savannah Morning News added that she fetched a Winchester rifle and that the man ran before she could fire.

Once the alarm was raised, "posses of citizens" searched for the man, who was located at several places and escaped each time before he was captured. The dispatch placed the capture on the afternoon of March 8 about five miles south of Parish, while the Palatka News and Advertiser said only that he was taken "several miles from town" and brought back. He was taken to the scene of the alleged crime and hanged to a tree that night.

The wire report said the hanging followed his positive identification by the girl and his admission of guilt, but no account names any member of the posses or describes how the confession was obtained. According to the Palatka paper, citizens found his body "dangling" from the tree the next morning. No report of an inquest, an arrest or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press item, datelined Tampa, March 9, ran that day and the next in papers from Illinois and Iowa to Maine, Indiana and Kentucky, usually as a two-sentence notice under heads such as "Negro Lynched in Florida." Some prints garbled the place as "Paris" or the dateline as "Tampa, Ala.," and the Rock Island Argus headed it "A Negro Fiend Is Lynched in Florida."

Southern papers printed the longer version under headlines that treated the hanging as deserved punishment: the Birmingham Age-Herald ran "Negro Lynched for Usual Crime" over "Wretch Admitted Guilt," the Richmond Times-Dispatch "Negro Meets Punishment for the Usual Crime," and the Newberry Herald and News "Fate of a Brutal Negro who Attacked a Little White Girl."

In Florida, the Ocala Banner reprinted the full dispatch and the Palatka News and Advertiser gave the episode a short paragraph in its state news digest, the only report to name Manatee County. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress, without naming Thomas, wrote that he would "doubtless" have been legally hanged had his case come to trial, but that the people "did not have the patience to wait its slow progress." Mid-year tallies of "mob law" in white papers reduced the case to "Negro hanged, Tampa, Fla., March 10."

In the Black press the lynching appears only in a "Record of Lynchings" credited to The Striker, which the Wichita Searchlight printed in July and the Sedalia Times in August 1903. That list named "Henry Thomas, colored, criminal assault," dated the lynching March 9 and placed it in "Parish, Ala.," among the 48 men it counted as killed by "lawless men" since January 1.

Reports differ on the charge: most say he "attempted" an assault, while the leads in the Americus and Ocala papers say he "criminally assaulted" the girl although their own text describes an attempt she escaped. Later lists give the date as March 9 or 10 and place it at Tampa, the wire dateline, or in Alabama, against the dispatches' Sunday night, March 8, near Parish.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Thomas
bases: Citizen posses captured Henry Thomas on an accusation of attempted assault and hanged him to a tree near Parish without any legal proceeding (A1, A3, A12).

Thomas was hanged to a tree by 'posses of citizens' (plural) who had hunted and captured him, with no officer or court involved, as punishment for an alleged attempted assault on a child (A3, A4, A12); the wire's 'admitted his guilt' and a Mississippi editorial's remark that he would 'doubtless' have been legally hanged frame it as summary justice (A1, A15).

The Associated Press dispatch from Tampa (A1, A3, A4) and the Palatka News and Advertiser's Florida digest, which adds details absent from the wire (Manatee county, Sunday night, body found next morning) (A12), agree on the victim, accusation, place and hanging; the Black-press lists (A19, A20) derive from a separate compilation.
